title: Sets, Relations and Functions
prerequisites: Familiarity with the idea of a collection of objects.
Understanding of ordered pairs and the Cartesian plane.
Ability to substitute into an algebraic expression.
Knowledge of number systems N, Z, Q and R.

topics.title: Sets and Set Operations
topics.quick_summary: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, and sets are combined using union, intersection, difference and complement.
topics.real_life: A search filter showing items that are 'in stock AND under ₹500' is computing the intersection of two sets.

detailed.definition: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The union A ∪ B contains elements in A or B or both; the intersection A ∩ B contains elements in both; the difference A − B contains elements in A but not in B.
detailed.key_idea: 'Well-defined' means membership must be decidable without opinion. 'The set of tall students' is not a set; 'the set of students above 170 cm' is.
detailed.working_principle: Venn diagrams turn set identities into pictures, and the inclusion–exclusion principle n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B) corrects for the double counting of the overlap.
applications: A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ and (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′.
Disjoint sets have no common element, so A ∩ B = ∅.

points: Elements of a set are distinct and unordered — {1,2,2,3} is just {1,2,3}.
The empty set ∅ is a subset of every set.
A set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets and 2ⁿ − 1 proper subsets.
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
De Morgan's laws exchange union and intersection under complementation.
mistakes: Listing repeated elements in a set.
Forgetting to subtract n(A ∩ B) and double counting the overlap.
topics.memory_hook: 'Union is OR, Intersection is AND' — and subtract the overlap once to stop counting it twice.
topics.advanced: Naive set theory permits Russell's paradox — the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Modern mathematics avoids it with axiomatic set theory, which restricts how sets may be formed.

topics.title: Relations and Functions
topics.quick_summary: A relation is any set of ordered pairs, and a function is a relation in which each input has exactly one output.
topics.real_life: A student's roll number maps to exactly one name, which makes it a function; a name might match several roll numbers, so the reverse is only a relation.

detailed.definition: A relation R from set A to set B is a subset of the Cartesian product A × B. A function f : A → B is a relation in which every element of A is associated with exactly one element of B.
detailed.key_idea: Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function. The distinguishing test is that no input may have two different outputs.
detailed.working_principle: The vertical line test applies this graphically: if any vertical line meets the graph more than once, the relation is not a function.
applications: If n(A) = m and n(B) = n, then n(A × B) = mn and there are 2^(mn) relations from A to B.
Domain = set of all inputs; Range = set of actual outputs; Codomain = the target set B.
One-one (injective), onto (surjective) and one-one onto (bijective) classify functions.

points: A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B.
A function assigns exactly one output to each input.
Domain, codomain and range must be distinguished; the range is a subset of the codomain.
Vertical line test: more than one intersection means it is not a function.
Number of relations from A to B is 2^(mn) where m and n are the sizes of A and B.
mistakes: Assuming a function cannot give the same output for two different inputs — it can, unless it is one-one.
topics.memory_hook: 'One input, one output' — that single rule separates functions from relations.
topics.advanced: Defining a function as a set of ordered pairs removes any appeal to a 'rule' or 'formula', which matters because most functions cannot be written as a formula at all. This set-theoretic definition is what modern analysis is built on.
